title: Thyroid and parathyroid glands (posterior)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender; surface detail added with an image model.

rows: Front of the neck. Its two lobes lie beside the larynx and trachea and are joined by an isthmus across the 2nd to 4th tracheal rings.
Its follicular cells make the thyroid hormones T3 and T4, which set the metabolic rate. Its parafollicular (C) cells make calcitonin.
Superior thyroid artery, from the external carotid artery, and inferior thyroid artery, from the thyrocervical trunk.
hy: It forms at the back of the tongue (foramen cecum) and descends along the thyroglossal duct. A thyroglossal duct cyst is a midline neck lump that moves up when the tongue is stuck out.
Thyroid surgery puts the recurrent laryngeal nerves (hoarseness) and the parathyroid glands (low blood calcium) at risk.

rows: Behind the upper or middle part of the lobe of the thyroid gland.
Secretes parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium by acting on bone, kidney and, through vitamin D, the gut.
hy: Develops from the 4th pharyngeal pouch.
In DiGeorge syndrome the 3rd and 4th pouches fail to develop: no parathyroids (low blood calcium) and no thymus (T-cell deficiency).

hy: Develops from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch, together with the thymus. It starts higher than the superior gland and ends lower.

rows: Runs from the cricoid cartilage at C6 to its division into the two main bronchi at the level of the sternal angle. The esophagus lies behind it.
Carries air to and from the lungs. C-shaped rings of cartilage hold it open, and the gap at the back is closed by the trachealis muscle.
hy: In the most common form of tracheoesophageal fistula the upper esophagus ends blindly and the lower esophagus opens into the trachea; the newborn drools, chokes and turns blue with the first feed.

rows: Below the thyroid cartilage at the level of C6, where the larynx becomes the trachea and the pharynx becomes the esophagus. It is shaped like a signet ring, narrow in front and tall behind.
Forms the base of the larynx and carries the arytenoid cartilages. It is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway.
Largest cartilage of the larynx, at the level of C4 to C5. Its two plates meet in front at the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple).
Shields the front of the larynx. The vocal ligaments attach to the back of the angle between its plates, and its inferior horns hinge on the cricoid cartilage.
Front of the neck at the level of C3, between the mandible and the larynx. It is U-shaped.
No other bone. It is held in place by muscles and ligaments, with the thyrohyoid membrane joining it to the larynx.
Body with greater and lesser horns. It anchors the tongue and the suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles.
hy: A fractured hyoid in an adult suggests strangulation.

rows: Leaf-shaped elastic cartilage behind the root of the tongue and the hyoid bone, attached by its stalk to the inside of the thyroid cartilage.
Folds back over the entrance to the larynx during swallowing and keeps food out of the airway.
hy: Epiglottitis, classically due to Haemophilus influenzae type b in an unvaccinated child, causes fever, drooling and noisy breathing; a swollen epiglottis shows as a thumbprint on a lateral X-ray of the neck.

rows: One of a pair of small pyramids sitting on the upper edge of the back of the cricoid cartilage.

Its vocal process anchors the vocal ligament and its muscular process receives the cricoarytenoid muscles. Rotating and sliding on the cricoid, the two cartilages open and close the gap between the vocal folds.
hy: The posterior cricoarytenoid muscles, which attach here, are the only muscles that open the vocal folds.

rows: Small nodule on the tip of each arytenoid cartilage, inside the aryepiglottic fold.
Stiffens and supports the aryepiglottic fold.

Thyrocervical trunk, a branch of the subclavian artery.
Ascends and then arches medially behind the carotid sheath to the lower pole of the thyroid gland.
Lower part of the thyroid gland, usually all four parathyroid glands, and parts of the larynx, trachea and esophagus.
hy: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs close to this artery near the lower pole of the thyroid and can be injured when the artery is tied off in thyroid surgery, causing hoarseness.

rows: Upper part of the thyroid gland. It runs with the superior thyroid artery.
Upper part of the thyroid gland. It runs with the superior thyroid artery.
On the right, the brachiocephalic trunk. On the left, the aortic arch directly.
Ascends in the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve and divides at about the upper border of the thyroid cartilage into the internal and external carotid arteries.
Head and neck, through its two end branches. It has no other branches.
hy: At its division lie the carotid sinus, a baroreceptor, and the carotid body, a chemoreceptor; both signal mainly through the glossopharyngeal nerve.

rows: Brain, face and neck. It begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus.
Descends in the carotid sheath, lateral to the carotid arteries and the vagus nerve.
Joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
hy: The height of its pulsation (jugular venous pressure) reflects right atrial pressure and rises in right heart failure.

rows: Medulla. It leaves the skull through the jugular foramen.
Descends in the carotid sheath between the internal jugular vein and the carotid artery, then through the chest to the abdomen along the esophagus.

Muscles of the palate (except tensor veli palatini), the pharynx (except stylopharyngeus) and the larynx; parasympathetic fibers to the heart, the lungs and the gut as far as the splenic flexure; sensation from the larynx and the viscera.
hy: With a vagus lesion the uvula deviates away from the side of the lesion, the voice is hoarse and swallowing is impaired.

rows: The right nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery; the left hooks under the aortic arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum. Both ascend in the groove between the trachea and the esophagus to the larynx.
All the intrinsic muscles of the larynx except cricothyroid, and sensation below the vocal folds.
hy: Injury causes hoarseness; injury on both sides can close the airway. It is at risk in thyroid surgery, and the left nerve can be compressed in the chest by an aortic arch aneurysm, an enlarged left atrium or a tumor.
